You may wonder, as do I, and as do people everywhere: how could this great scholar have gained access to such truth, when all of the earlier scholars and the great guides and imams failed to do so? I would reply to you: a person has nothing except what they strive for

Indeed, people are differentiated through their actions.

This is true even for the Envoys (Messengers) and noble Prophets... and there will be a different level for everyone according to their deeds in this world.

Our own great scholar Mohammad Amin Sheikho was given awareness and understanding by Al’lah, and he was distinguished by his outstanding deeds and his great and humane sacrifices. Al’lah did not give him anything except that which he deserved.

chapters.title: The French Weapons of Anjar Citadel Are Taken by Syrian Rebels
chapters.html:
During the French occupation of Syria our officer, Mohammad Amin Sheikho, became a regional manager for Anjar Castle which was situated in the border region between Syria and Lebanon. He was appointed to this eminent position for his renowned abilities as a remarkable leader. This castle was used as a temporary arsenal for weapons being trans-shipped through Lebanon, as well as being an important centre and stronghold against the Syrian insurgents.

It happened that the French government sent a large consignment of various kinds of weapons and ammunition to supply its military forces in Syria and Lebanon who were tasked with suppressing the insurgency and other minor uprisings wherever they broke out.

The consignment of war materiel was shipped from France and transported to the castle in the border territory where it was stored pending its distribution to the French forces in Syria.

When the shipment arrived at Anjar Castle the weapons became the sole responsibility of the officer who was in charge of the security of the castle.

Despite having been entrusted with such a high position by the French, Officer Sheikho’s loyalties lay with the rebels who were fighting to liberate their country. And so, he resolved to deliver the weapons to the Syrian insurgents, who were the enemies of the French government, even though he risked losing his own life for what the French would see as the worst possible betrayal.

He duly informed the insurgents and instructed them to start removing the arms under the cover of darkness. Accordingly, he gave leave of absence to some policemen whom he felt unable to trust and told his loyal men to remain on duty along with his faithful adjutant. When night fell and darkness prevailed, the rebels came and began to remove the weapons from the castle under cover of the dark, cloudy sky.

After midnight, the ingenious officer called the commanderin- chief to tell him that the castle had come under attack by a large and powerful force of rebels, ‘The castle’s under attack... my men are fighting back bravely but they’re outnumbered... it’s a major skirmish... the rebels are bent on breaking into the castle, so... hurry... send reinforcements...!’

He had previously ordered his policemen to fire continuously into the air for the local villagers to hear; and he had arranged with the mayor of the village to say that he, Officer Sheikho, had actually sought his help, but that he was unable to offer any assistance because he lacked fighting power as the villagers were merely unarmed farmers. When the French forces, which Officer Sheikho had purposely summoned too late, arrived at the castle, they found that the rebels had emptied the storerooms of every last weapon and piece of ammunition, and had escaped with their spoils, successfully and safely.

When the news of this great catastrophe reached the French commissioner, General Catroux, he was so overcome with rage and aversion towards Officer Sheikho that he felt as though he would pass out. He did not believe the account that the castle had come under attack, and without any doubt he considered that the officer’s actions amounted to high treason. How had Officer Sheikho dared to deliver an entire shipment of weaponry and ammunition to the rebels? It was the greatest military shipment the French government had ever sent to Syria; this vast amount had been necessary after the French army had used up most of its ammunition and war materiel against the insurgents. A most worrying thought came to General Catroux: what would he say to his government? He became so angry that he lost all sense of reason and immediately sentenced both Officer Sheikho and his adjutant to summary execution.

That very night, they were brought to Damascus to be executed at dawn the following day, as was the usual procedure. But, what a miracle! Despite facing the death penalty our officer showed no sign of fear or cowardice, for he felt that his actions at the castle had been right and fully justified, and the expected results would inevitably bring about good for everyone: for the real Doer is Al’lah.

Mohammad Amin actually lay down in the locked cell feeling completely at ease and tranquil and drifted into a restful sleep.

Al’lah says, “Remember! He made you drowsy as a reassurance from Him.” ﴿2﴾

His adjutant, in fear for their lives woke him saying, ‘We’re condemned to death and you’re sleeping! Don’t you know that we’re going to be executed in a few hours? How can you even think about sleep?’ He started to clap his hands together, over and over again, crying and shouting, ‘Oh, my sons! Who will take care of you when I’m gone?’ He was pacing back and forth across the cell as if he had lost his mind, then he turned towards our officer repeating yet again, ‘How can you sleep when we’re going to be executed at dawn?’

Trying to resist sleep and feeling overcome with joy and certain confidence our officer replied, ‘I’m perfectly happy, and sleep seems so desirable... I can’t keep my eyes open. I can think of nothing but sleep... so please... just let me sleep!’

When he heard these words from his superior officer and saw him settling down to sleep again, he burst into tears and began to wail, ‘Oh, my sons! My wife!... What will you do after my death?... What will happen to you?’

He was truly suffering from such overwhelming fear and his heart was broken at the thought of what a bleak future his family would face. The light seemed to go out of his eyes, and he remained in this sorry state until the new day dawned. On the other hand our officer, Mohammad Amin, slept soundly and happily, seemingly without a care in the world, and giving no thought at all to the impending execution.

When they were driven to the place of execution at dawn, the French commander was still enraged, so he went out of the gate of the government house to see the officers who had been condemned to death, for not only had they lost and destroyed France’s ammunitions and military supplies in Syria, they had actually delivered them into the hands of his enemy.

As the two condemned men were passing in front of the government house (al-Saraya ﴿3﴾

he glared at them with a look of intense fury, but at the same time it occurred to him that he should speak to them. So he ordered the military escort to bring the two men before him for he wanted to try to understand the character of Officer Sheikho and discern how that huge loss had occurred, and how he had dared to carry out this shocking action. But catching sight of the courageous officer coming towards him with his head held high, and his strong steady steps denoting his great pride and fearsome strength of character, the commander was filled with a confused sense of wonder combined with condemnation.

Officer Sheikho strode towards him, his face wreathed in smiles, as though he were a man hurrying to his own wedding. The French commander was so confused that he was about to explode... unable to believe what he saw with his own eyes. He could not stop himself from crying out in a quivering voice, ‘What happened to you? What about that great act of treason you are guilty of? You delivered our weapons to the enemy!’

Brimming with confidence and free from any sense of fear, our officer replied in a firm, calm voice, ‘The rebels attacked us, and a great skirmish broke out between them and my policemen which lasted for many hours. I asked your Syrian commander-in-chief for reinforcements and told him that the rebels were very strong and well organised and that we would not be able to defend the castle for much longer. That help was not forthcoming so, I asked the village mayor for whatever assistance he could offer but he had no arms or men to help us to confront the rebel forces. So, as we were not given any reinforcements, and after a suicidal fight bravely fought by my men, the insurgents managed to break into the castle after a lengthy one-sided battle. After that, I had no choice but to order my men to retreat through the secret underground passage.’

The Syrian commandant was sitting near the French general, the commander of the French forces in Syria, who turned to the Syrian and asked, ‘Did this officer really inform you about the serious situation at the castle and ask for help?’

At that point, the Syrian commander, whose thoughts were focused on other matters, failed to understand the question which had been directed at him and he replied simply, ‘Yes.’ When the French general realised what the Syrian commandant had said, he regained his senses, and his intense anger abated. He became deeply absorbed in his thoughts, ‘So, this officer was not responsible for what happened, and in fact he carried out his duties perfectly and faithfully.’

After the general had angrily asked for his opinion about their Syrian police leader, Mohammad Amin continued speaking and replied to the general, ‘Do you really think that you have a high commander? This man is good for nothing but selling beans, so how could he be suitable to hold the position of high commander of the police and armed forces?’

The general turned to the interpreter to ask for an explanation, ‘What does he mean by a beans vendor?’

He replied, ‘Do you remember, sir, when we were touring the country during the Greater Bairam, ﴿4﴾

when we saw a slovenly old man with a dirty fez on his head and a pot of boiled beans before him... and beside him there was a table with small stools around, and little children eating beans? Do you remember how you laughed at this odd sight? This is what this officer meant by a beans vendor.’

The general had found the sight of that old man very amusing when he first saw him selling beans from a barrow, and as soon as he remembered the occasion and heard the comparison of the vendor with the Syrian high commander of the police and armed forces, he burst into convulsive laughter: his entire demeanour became relaxed and a look of pleasure and delight seemed etched clearly on his face.

Indeed, with this spontaneous burst of laughter, the terrible crisis and the awful threat of the sentence of execution were dispelled as the general picked up the telephone receiver and called the French commissioner who was also still enraged, and had passed sleepless nights because of the great disaster that had befallen them. He addressed him saying, ‘Your Excellency, General Catroux! We were about to execute our most loyal supporter and his adjutant, because of our angry outburst, but they are completely blameless.’ And he told him about the incident as he had heard it from our officer.

While the French general was scrutinizing our officer, Mohammad Amin, from head to toe, he suddenly popped a clever question at him saying, ‘On your honour as a military man, tell me the truth! Are you really happy with our occupation of your country?’

Our erudite officer replied, ‘Truly, I wish our roles were reversed and that I could take your place in Paris, and that my country could govern yours.’ Yet after this astonishing reply, he continued by complimenting the general, saying... ‘but, since we (the Arabs) are underdeveloped, and the League of Nations Assembly has given you a mandate over us to spread civilisation in our country, to help it to develop and make progress, I am satisfied!’

The general admired his reply and said, ‘That’s true! Really, you’re an honest citizen who is loyal to his country, as well as to us. Truly, you rank very highly in our eyes and are exonerated, in our consideration; you may return to your office now, with our thanks and praise for your heroic defence!’

But our officer asked the general to discharge him from his post, so the general, astonished, asked him why he should make that request.

He replied, ‘If I retain my position in your police corps after I spoke as I did about that high commandant, he will surely scheme and plot against me to regain the esteem and position he previously held, and since his rank is higher than mine, you will undoubtedly believe him.’

Yet the general refused to discharge him saying, ‘You’ll stay on duty, and I’ll refuse to listen to a single bad word about you... from anyone!’

Our officer then took his leave, and no sooner had he walked away from the government house with his adjutant and they felt perfectly safe, than the latter embraced him with tears in his eyes saying, ‘You have just saved our lives, my friend!’

But, when our officer heard that, he knelt down and his mind was full of the thoughts of who was truly responsible for the positive outcome, ‘Al’lah... it is Al’lah Who really did it... by God! It was as if with luminous letters written on the wall behind and above the general, Al’lah showed me both the question and the answer: what I would be asked and what I should reply.’

Certainly, for the one who sees by Al’lah’s Light, He always prepares a way out and eases his difficulty, so, see by Al’lah’s Light and He will surely teach you!

chapters.title: Man’s Loyalty to His Country Is Paramount
chapters.html:
The Prophet Mohammad (cpth ﴿5﴾

said,

“Faith brings about patriotism.”

During the French occupation of our country, Mohammad Amin Sheikho contrived many refined and unrivalled plans, by which he put an end to the wrongs done to its people, which they had neither realised nor expected.

Clearly, he stood by all that was true and the proponents of peace and justice, and he did his utmost to expel oppression and corruption from the country. This is the account of one of the commendable stratagems which he adopted.

Once, our officer, who held the rank of first lieutenant, made a thorough study concerning a particular matter and came to the conclusion that it should be implemented because of the anticipated positive result it would achieve. But there was something rather strange about this affair.

A certain French officer of the same rank as Officer Sheikho did all that he could to thwart him in the execution of that legitimate undertaking! Although Mohammad Amin gave him a full explanation of its advantages and the legality of his plans, he insisted on maintaining his blind opposition. He was adamant that the matter could not be accomplished.

Our officer was mounted on his horse whilst having this conversation with the French officer who was standing nearby, seemingly full of his own self-importance and treating the words of our officer with utter contempt. Mohammad Amin pondered the reason for his stubborn opinion and could see right through it, ‘He wants to force his opinion and wishes upon me out of his feeling of superiority; because he is a French officer he thinks that I am inferior to him... nothing but an inferior Arab! Even though this matter is none of his business, and his attitude actually contravenes French law! So, he’s being bull-headed and opposing my plan just for the sake of it! O.K... I’ll show you, you proud officer!’

He remained as he was, sitting on his horse, motionless, turning over in his mind the conclusion he had just reached. Suddenly, he raised his head and gently prodded his horse’s flanks; she took a few steps forward then he reined her in beside the French officer who was still standing looking at him with an air of great disdain. Leaping from the back of his horse, he boldly confronted the French officer by encircling him with one arm and in one swift movement he drew his revolver and pointed the barrel at the officer’s head, with no regard whatsoever for him or his government, and said, ‘You! French officer! My plans will be carried out.’ Then he spat out the words, ‘So don’t poke your nose where it isn’t needed... otherwise...’

The French officer had his heart in his boots, as he thought he was about to die. He appeared to crumple before Officer Sheikho and answered in a trembling voice, ‘A... a... as... as you like... as you like.’

Actually, the lawful matter we mentioned earlier was executed precisely according to Officer Sheikho’s plan, and the successful outcome was as he had anticipated.

But what about the Syrian’s insult to one of the ruling French officers? Could it be ignored? Should it go without punishment... especially as it was issued by an Arab officer?

The French first lieutenant ﴿6﴾

considered his humiliation at the hands of the Arab officer an insult to his country, France, and in defiance of its government! This was the illinspired opinion of the French officer even though Officer Sheikho’s actions had been correct and lawful.

The prestige and courage of our officer, Mohammad Amin Sheikho, were a strong deterrent that prevented the French officer from trying to avenge himself face to face. He thought it wise not to approach Officer Sheikho in public, so made sure to keep his distance. Therefore, he resorted to the machinery of his government in Syria and informed senior French officers about the incident, which infuriated them.

They, in turn, informed General Catroux, but French legislation prevented them meting out any punishment to Officer Sheikho, or even reprimanding him, because the action he had executed was in the course of his assigned duties. The meddling of the French officer, however, was wrong and clearly an unwarranted encroachment, therefore they had no legitimate reason to censure Officer Sheikho, otherwise they would damage their own reputation, which would reflect badly on them.

The French came to our country and occupied it under the guise of a mandate authorised by the League of Nations so as to help us to advance and keep pace with the process of development and civilisation in all fields. That was their rationale; so if they did not abide by the law, they would lose face which, ultimately, would go against them.

Therefore, they planned to punish Mohammad Amin, or even to get rid of him, by clever subterfuge. They doubted his loyalty to them, so they decided to plot against him. They sent him to the motherland of the revolutionary insurgency, the Druzes’ district on al-Arab Mountain, where the Great Syrian revolution was gaining strength day by day.

The written orders were issued for his appointment and he went there as an area commander with a company of soldiers delegated to accompany him so that the assignment would seem routine and not instigated by nefarious motives. The French thought that the revolutionaries would be sure to kill him because he was an officer... but as we shall learn, their plan failed!

On the day he was due to leave, Mohammad Amin mounted his horse and rode to the head of the column to lead his men out of the barracks. He fully understood the reason for these military orders but he did not care, for he had put his trust in God. He was well aware of the purpose of this order, for which he was prepared, and was sure that it would be accomplished.

The troop proceeded along the road following their leader, heading for the Druzes’ district. They walked for a long time until eventually they approached the boundaries of the area. There was a valley running between two mountains which was controlled by the Druze insurgents; an ambush was quickly prepared for the troops after the Druzes received information that they had passed through the valley, and they came under heavy fire from the insurgents.

Oh God! It was a perilous situation! There was no cover to protect them from the Druze barrage, and if they advanced even one more step they would be under fire... what should they do?

The commandant, Officer Mohammad Amin, quickly assessed the situation and decided that the best way to secure a safe shelter for his men was to take cover with his soldiers at the foot of the mountain and conceal themselves behind the many large boulders there. So, he quickly ordered his company to move in that direction which gave them immediate cover from the revolutionaries’ gunfire.

Then, realising that this was the safest place, our officer ordered them, ‘Stay here while I go ahead to explore the valley... perhaps I’ll find a passage out of range of their fire... don’t move until I come back.’

He spurred his horse on and drove it through a narrow, rough passage between the rocks, keeping out of sight of the rebels until he was some distance from his own troops, and then he reappeared in full view of the rebels. But before that, he took the precautionary measure of tearing a piece from his white shirt and tying it to the barrel of his gun; he then held the gun aloft showing the make-shift white flag of truce indicating that he came with peaceful intentions.

The insurgents saw the flag swinging from the officer’s rifle, so they immediately sent five or six of their men down from their hideout on the mountain, drawing their firearms as they went, so as to meet the commandant, Officer Sheikho. He addressed them, ‘It’s true that I’m an officer in the enemy government but I am a rebel like you, and here is the seal of the revolution.’ He mentioned to them some signs and symbols and certain passwords which were known to no-one but the rebels.

The men quickly realised the truth of his words and were happy to see that such an eminent personality was one of them... one of the revolutionaries. They looked at one another with an air of confidence which clearly conveyed that they believed his words. Then, one of them who appeared to be the head of this small group spoke out, ‘So, men, we have to stop shooting, for this magnanimous officer is a true rebel and very important to our cause...’

‘No, you fearless rebel,’ Mohammad Amin interrupted him, ‘the French are spying on me. They don’t trust my loyalty to them and have doubts about my dealings with you. So you have to continue firing, but aim to miss. Then at night you can let us pass. In this way, the spies will see that we met with great resistance from you... and that will ensure my safety and will also be favourable for the revolution; French suspicions will be allayed and consequently I’ll be able to continue my plans and have a greater chance of success.’

Having heard these logical words, the leader of the revolutionary group replied, ‘Yes, you’re right... O.k. brave officer, we agree.’

They shook hands and there were smiles all round as they sealed their peaceful cooperation. Then, the man turned to his friends and said, ‘Let’s go men!’

They all turned back pleased with what they had achieved and left to rejoin the rest of the rebels who were waiting in their hideout on the mountain, eager to know what had transpired with the officer during their parley down below.

There and then, they resumed their firing but aimed at false targets as Mohammad Amin had instructed them to do. Meanwhile, our officer returned safely to his outfit and gave orders to his men to stay where they were until nightfall.

Then, as evening came and the shooting stopped he led them through winding pathways down in the valley and entered the town; but on his way to the police station he took a circuitous route in order to cover their tracks and avoid the rebels’ fire until they finally reached the safety of the police station and settled in. Thus, the French authorities could find no evidence to accuse him of any breach of duty or that he was supporting the rebels.

The next day, our officer was sitting in his new office in the county headquarters when a Druze peasant from the town requested permission to speak to him. When the man entered the office, he said to our officer, ‘Sir, I want to tell you something in confidence... it’s very important!’

‘What is it? Come on, tell me.’

‘Sir, some smugglers will pass close to this area driving a train of camels...’

Before he had finished, our officer felt a burst of anger flare up in his chest. He leaped to his feet and roared at the man, ‘Right now, the weight of the enemy is hanging over our heads... they’re occupying our lands, taking all the benefits and blessings of our country... they’re oppressing our people and spreading corruption and misery... and you have come here to inform on a train of camel smugglers! What’s the problem? Don’t you see how much our people are suffering from the oppression of foreign occupation?’

Officer Sheikho was speaking in a forceful, angry tone of voice and as he spat out the words he was edging gradually closer to the peasant who was shuffling backwards, his face grown pale with fear because of the menacing face of the officer before him. Suddenly, our officer dashed towards him causing him to turn around and rush away as fast as his legs would carry him. His only thought was to escape from the enraged officer and he did not stop, even to retrieve his kaffiyeh ﴿7﴾

which had fallen from his head, until he had put the county headquarters well behind him and disappeared into the warren of alleyways in the town.

In the evening of that same day, the second day that Mohammad Amin had been in the town, beacons were lit on the surrounding mountaintops one after another so that the flames and smoke rose high in the sky to be seen clearly by all.

In fact, that peasant who went to report the story of the camel train to our officer was one of the rebels. The local leaders of the revolution had sent him to check the loyalty of the new area commander. Not only did the French spy on him but the rebels did so too! They wanted to assure themselves of his allegiance to them and his true attitude concerning France, so they fabricated the story of smugglers to test him. When they were sure of his reaction, they lit a bonfire on the mountain top as a pre-arranged signal to all the Druzes of the town that the new area-manager was a rebel too, and therefore their ally, so they should all go along with him and his plans. Thus, all the local insurgents knew that the Arab commander, Mohammad Amin Sheikho, was a patriot and a loyal rebel of great importance and great assistance to them against France.

From that time on, they began to work closely with him in all matters concerning the insurgency. They never once mounted an attack against the French forces or their arsenals and war materials without resorting to his unique genius in military planning and management. Then, whenever they launched an attack, Mohammad Amin never failed to inform the French military command about it... but always too late! The insurgents were able to finish their incursion and return safely with their spoils before the arrival of the French forces.

And, in the estimation of the French, the officer was considered irreproachable since he informed them about an attack as soon as he knew about it; he carried out his duty perfectly, and was loyal to them, so they duly thanked him! In that way, the brave patriotic officer was able to work on behalf of his homeland and help his people against their enemy. He was the iron fist for the revolutionaries and at the same time a trustworthy officer for the French by reason of his wonderful experience in all areas of military management.

This episode brings to mind the ancient military treatise, “The Art of War”.

chapters.title: Lack of Commitment Leads to Failure of the Revolution
chapters.html:
Officer Sheikho seemed to be totally preoccupied with an extremely weighty matter. His features were clouded by serious, deep contemplation, while a look of intense truthfulness and firm determination could be seen in his eyes.

His spirit was always fully absorbed in finding the way to express a flood of great compassion and kindness. So, a few lines had appeared as furrows on his wide, pale brow indicating the breadth of vision associated with his lofty intentions that paid no heed to the passage of time and its many events; equally they denoted the lines of the future inscribed on the pages of history.

Hovering close by was a soldier waiting to speak to the officer, but he hesitated to disturb him. He, too, appeared to have a pressing problem on his mind and stood there sighing from time to time. Eventually, he approached his commandant pleading, ‘Sir... sir, please, I want leave of absence.’

Mohammad Amin snapped out of his reverie, ‘What? Leave of absence!’ he thought. He could not believe his ears! ‘You’re asking for leave as we’re about to set off on a mission! Are you crazy? Get away from me!’

The soldier left, wrapped in his own thoughts once again. But it must be said that this soldier was extremely fond of his commanding officer and trusted him implicitly; he saw in him all the characteristics of bravery, manhood and humanity, so he turned his horse once again towards him and said, ‘Please, sir! I beg you to let me go now, and I will join you tomorrow. I know the area where you will pitch camp... it is at the end of Damascus Oasis, it is... ‘and he began to describe the exact location to his commandant, then he continued, ‘So, I promise you, sir, upon my honour that I will keep my word.’

‘What are you saying? How can you ask for leave at this time? Does this mean that you are a coward and afraid to die? If I agree to your request it will be as if I’m giving you permission to stay away from danger, to be safe from dying, and if this gets to the ears of the high command they will charge me with treason. And then we’ll both be sentenced to death.’

‘Sir, I’m appealing to your leniency, and call for your kindness and compassion to let me go. My wife is now suffering the pains of childbirth and her delivery is usually difficult; and as you know, sir, I am a foreigner in this country and have no family or friends here, so there is nobody to help her except me.’

‘Soldier! I have told you, go away! Under the circumstances no-one could possibly agree to such a request.’

The soldier turned away overcome with sadness, but before long he turned back towards his officer yet again, his source of refuge and support, but before he reached him an idea had flashed into the mind of our officer, Mohammad Amin, who was so overcome with happiness at finding a solution that an immense feeling of gratitude towards God seemed to shine from his eyes.

So, as the soldier approached him again, he winked at him to put him at ease, and then both of them spurred their horses and walked side by side away from the path of the column of scouts and military personnel, so as to be away from prying eyes.

‘I have thought about your problem,’ our officer said to the soldier, ‘and I really sympathise with you. I can feel how anxious and confused you are, so I’ve decided to give you an extended leave of absence. Go to your wife because I’m sure she needs some help, and perhaps her condition is dangerous for both her and the child; and do not return to duty until I send for you. But you, in turn, must do something for me.’

Eager to comply with his officer’s wishes the soldier said, ‘You have only to ask, sir, whatever you want, and you will find me at your service.’

‘In a little while we will reach the location which will be our base from where we’ll conduct exploratory forays. You know the area well, so I want you to...’ and he began to explain an idea he had in mind, while the soldier listened attentively. When our officer finished talking the soldier asked, ‘But sir! You haven’t told me what you want me to do.’

‘I’ll tell you when I send for you.’

The soldier thought that he wanted him to carry out a personal favour, so our officer left him with this false supposition and ordered him to rejoin his platoon.

The soldier spurred his horse and trotted away happily, his eyes filled with tears of joy.

Our officer, Mohammad Amin Sheikho, was a deputy commander of the French advance reconnaissance division, but if the high command had not been doubtful of his loyalty they would have assigned him as its commander. They were fully aware of his military genius and abilities that astounded them and caused them to admire him greatly; but, however, they could not forget that he was the officer in charge of Anjar Castle when the greatest arms deal between France and Greater Syria had taken place. These armaments had been stored in the castle and one night they were seized by the revolutionaries. The French could not be sure about his real role in that incident so they appointed him as an adjutant, rather than the commander.

The French government decided that it could no longer tolerate the revolutionaries’ skirmishes against its forces which kept them constantly on the alert, therefore they mounted this exploratory expedition of three thousand heavily armed soldiers, planning to exterminate all of the rebels once their locations and numbers had been established.

All members of the public came to know about this expedition, so a general air of gloominess and anxiety pervaded throughout society. Then the leaders of the revolution hurried as usual to their refuge, the Arab officer, Mohammad Amin Sheikho. How often had they reverted to him seeking his protection and found him, indeed, their strongest and safest sanctuary? How often had he endangered himself for their sake? And yet, every time they went back on their word and let him face his fate alone. Only Providence stood by him and saved him in the nick of time so that potential failure turned into unique success. But at this particular time, destruction and death were hovering above them, so they promised him faithfully and swore by God to measure up favourably in the judgement of their Lord and his. So, he did not disappoint them:

‘If God guides me to an appropriate solution I will certainly use it, but I am not the commander of this expedition, and the possibilities may be limited; so, put all your trust in God.’

The commanding officer of the reconnaissance expedition looked at his adjutant in a way that conveyed both trust and admiration. He knew of his expertise and wisdom and of his superb abilities for planning which led him to seek his advice on all military matters, and pin his faith on his genius. So, he gave no order without first asking his adjutant’s advice.

Therefore, when he saw that our officer had left the column to walk alongside a particular soldier he became concerned; yet it was not long until he saw him coming back towards him. Then, drawing an expression of sadness on his face, our officer spoke to him in a loud voice so as to let other soldiers hear, ‘l’m very surprised and feel rather anxious. I moved away from the column to explore the area and to question the herders so as to assess the best approach for the coming fight. I’ve been told that the rebels have come together from everywhere: from Aleppo, Idlib, Homs, Hama, and al-Arab Mountain, and they are all marching towards Damascus. They have called up a lot of supporters, numbering some ten thousand so far and it’s growing all the time. So, the information that the government has is true and not just rumour. Indeed, I cannot understand how they have sent us on this mission with such a small army. As the ruling power fighting against a gang of revolutionaries, shouldn’t we make a show of force and have three times as many men as they have in order not to lose face? Haven’t you noticed that the high command has not sent even one French man with us! But now talk is useless. We’re obliged to fight and win! In fact it’s obvious that this expedition is not for reconnaissance, as it’s supposed to be, but is for us to engage in combat.’

On hearing these words from his trusted adjutant, the commandant’s face turned pale and he was wide-eyed with shock. The news circulated among the ranks as rapidly as fire spreads through the dry stalks of a wheat field, and fear began to creep into their hearts.

The expedition continued marching until they reached the designated location. There, the soldiers hurried to set up camp. They pitched the commandant’s tent next to that of his adjutant after leaving a wide passage between them that divided the camp into two parts; then they put the arms in the middle standing on end and leaning one against the other creating pyramid-like shapes, so that the rifles could be quickly and easily accessed by the men.

When our officer entered his tent, the commandant hurried in behind him and asked, ‘What shall we do now? What is the fighting-plan?’

‘I’m tired now... in fact I feel exhausted, so I want to sleep for a couple of hours at least and then we can make plans. We are going to face a tough fight and we won’t be able to sleep tonight as the rebels are close.’ The commandant asked him in amazement, ‘Can you really sleep in such dangerous circumstances?’

‘Yes, why not?’ our officer replied and lay down on his camp bed and closed his eyes.

The commandant looked at him, his eyes wide with surprise, and then left the tent. He stood outside, completely bemused, brought out a bottle of wine and drank it to the last drop, then tossed the empty bottle away in frustration. He began to ply the area outside Mohammad Amin’s tent which made our officer feel a certain optimism; clearly he had no intention of sleeping but wanted to test the commandant’s reaction!

In the meantime, the soldier rode his horse slowly away from the camp and headed towards the hill behind which the camp was raised, and rode to the top; then he quickly turned his horse and spurred it on to gallop at full speed down the hill towards the camp.

The dust swirled and the horse neighed loudly then the sound of its thundering hoofs soon came to the ears of all the troops and their commander, and they sensed there must be danger in the air!

They all stood motionless and stared at the rapidly approaching rider who was waving his arms in the air, his face and eyes filled with dread. He was shouting but his words could not be understood.

As he passed through the passage between the tents of the commander and the adjutant his thunderous voice could be clearly heard and his terrible words fell on every ear, ‘We’ll be slayed, Arabs... we’ll be slayed, Arabs... we’ll be slayed...!’

The wilds seemed to echo the desperation in his voice, while he just kept on galloping, caring for nothing else!

The expedition leader looked startled and his eyes popped out, clearly showing the effects of the wine he had drunk. He looked towards our officer, the man of the moment, who rushed out of his tent and mounted his horse, loosened the reins and let it race away.

The soldiers turned their eyes towards the commandant and stared at him to see how he might react! But since he had been overcome by dismay and wine, in equal measure, he could think of nothing but saving his own skin; so he ran towards his horse and, mounting it, he spurred it into headlong flight. Silence and deadly alarm prevailed over the soldiers who stood there, their eyes wide with fear and terror!

What should they do?

Since the commandant and his adjutant had both fled, what could the soldiers do except turn tail and retreat? Suddenly, turmoil spread among them so that they seemed like a flock of sheep running away from the attack of a lion! The entire force, soldiers and officers, fled... caring for nothing but their own safety.

Indeed, the soldier who had requested leave of absence had now performed his part perfectly. He had been motivated by the vivid mental picture of his wife in labour and his concern that she might have difficulty while giving birth with no-one to help her... afraid that if he did not go to her he might lose her forever.

Now, let’s turn back to Officer Sheikho who continued to spur his horse to go even faster, and little by little, began to pull away from the line of the fleeing troops until he was sure that they could not see him. Then, he turned his horse back heading once again towards the camp. When he reached there, he rode about the camp and found nothing but complete quiet and empty tents. He looked at the dividing passage and saw the guns thrown to the ground in complete disarray. The cowardly troops had left everything behind and sought nothing but their own safety.

He dismounted his horse and set about looking for the field telephone; when he found it he cranked its handle a few turns and then asked to be put through to the high command. There and then, all other calls were interrupted and cut off, for calls from the front always had priority.

Within moments the interpreter was on the other end, translating every word to the French army commander who said to our officer eagerly, ‘Tell me: what is the news from you?’

‘It is very bad.’ our officer replied, ‘we’re having a hard time... there are more than ten thousand rebels coming at us from every direction and the number is increasing all the time, as if they’re pouring out of the land. So we have fallen back in order to avoid the rebels outflanking us so we could get out of this difficult position with minimal loss.’

‘But how can you be there talking to me?’ the French commander asked.

‘I have a racehorse...’

And immediately our officer cut the wire with a sharp knife that he had ready for this purpose, leaving the interpreter yelling, ‘Hello... hello...’ at the end of a dead line.

When the “defeated” troops reached Damascus, every one of them told a story about the event, his horror and fear inspired by his own imagination. So, they spoke about unbearable events filled with unbelievable violence. Besides, the majority of those men did not report back to their barracks, for they were sure that the occupying French would soon be driven out of the country by the assault of the revolutionaries; so they preferred to escape than to be killed.

This news was like a death blow for the French, for the high command thought that a great number of troops had been killed in the battle that, actually, did not take place! So, when General Sarrail, the French resident in Syria, looked into the reports and information which he received, he was shocked and overwhelmed with bitterness. He found himself in a desperate situation that filled him with terror, for he believed that in just one battle most of his troops had been killed while the revolutionaries were advancing in large numbers towards Damascus, hellbent on victory. This was the summary of the reports coming to him; therefore he believed that every opening had been closed to him and felt as though day had turned into night. He had not yet forgotten how the revolutionaries had attacked Anjar Castle and seized the weaponry and ammunition stored there which France had shipped to its army in Syria. At that moment, he turned to his general staff, and burst out in a bitter and desperate cry, ‘Pull out... pull out!’

All the French forces and their commanders withdrew to Lebanon and left everything behind: the barracks, the arsenals, the munitions, the bases, the mounted cannons with their balls at the crossroads, and guns scattered here and there.

They were happy to run away.

Even in Beirut, General Sarrail did not feel safe. He feared that the forces of the resistance would reach there to weaken French power and destroy them. Therefore, he preferred to make use of one of the warships which patrolled the Mediterranean Sea and to wait on board to watch the culmination of that horrible event.

Thus, Syria remained free of its occupiers and enemies for three full days and nights, waiting for honest Syrian men to seize the opportunity that Officer Sheikho had presented to them; it was the opportune moment for them to make the first move in order to shrug off the mantle of shame, and eliminate injustice.

But alas! Slaves are not shackled by their chains, but rather by their own subservience; their dubious intentions soon became clear and their lack of conscience obvious to everybody.

Is that not what you asked for?

Is that not what you wanted him to do?

Mohammad Amin accepted to go to fight alone with the support of his Lord; so after this distinct victory you had only to enter the empty barracks, take up the dust-covered ordnance and take over the country!

Instead of that, the revolutionaries headed for the stores and set about plundering them and killing each other; and one of the dishonest leaders of the revolution was killed while he was robbing a storekeeper in al-Bzouriyah market at gunpoint.

For three full days and nights every camp remained empty, with no-one present to offer any resistance; but even so, not a single positive idea passed between the leaders of the revolution, who surely, had failed to rise to the cause.

In the meantime, the agents who were in the pay of the French were following the situation, and informed them that no-one had entered their camps or touched their heavy armaments on the rebels behalf, and that the whole affair had been like nothing more than a dense black cloud that had passed without becoming a storm.

When General Sarrail received the news he returned to Syria with his army and vented his anger on Damascus; he did not hesitate to show the depths of his inhumanity and previously concealed bitterness and anger. He gave orders for the heavy artillery to shell the al-Midan quarter which was known as the refuge of the insurgents, so the houses were destroyed and the flames rose high into the sky, while rivers of blood flowed depriving children of their parents, and parents of their children: reflecting a picture of the most draconian barbarity

chapters.title: Our Man Rises to the Challenge in the Region of Al - Sheikh Mountain
chapters.html:
Our Man Rises to the Challenge in the Region of Al-Sheikh Mountain

The French state appointed Officer Mohammad Amin Sheikho as a regional manager of a certain district at al-Sheikh Mountain which was inhabited by the hierarchy of the Christian and Druze communities.

He set off to assume his task fully confident in God.

At the approach to the region, he met one of the local policemen, who happened to hold the rank of corporal. Characteristics of defiance, arrogance, and superiority were clearly written on the man’s face, and his anarchic military uniform served only to indicate his general air of disorder and lack of discipline. Even more annoying was the fact that this fool set about addressing Officer Sheikho with threats and foul language just to irritate and humiliate him, but our officer ignored him and acted as though he had heard nothing. This only encouraged the corporal to issue further menaces about what would happen if the officer did not submit to their will (i.e. the will of one or other side: the Christian or the Druze masters).

It was the initial confrontation and on the face of it the problem seemed to be serious, but Officer Sheikho was accustomed to winning through in every exploit he undertook as he relied upon He Who steers all matters... he relied upon Al’lah.

He simply bypassed the matter of that trouble-making corporal... but the wheels of his mind were turning at full speed. Then he reached the police-station assigned to him and found it to be in a deplorable condition: the offices, situated on the upper floor of an old house, were grimy, and an air of negligence pervaded every nook and cranny.

He went up to the previous commander’s old office via shaky wooden stairs... and on entering he found the dust thick on the desk... the ink dried to powder... all the records covered with dust: everything indicated the opposition which he would face in that place.

He quickly summed up the scenario and his intuition told him that there was a surreptitious, underlying situation here, and it would be necessary to use his intelligence to deal with the facts in order to achieve rational changes.

He stood there deep in thought for this was the only way forward given the facts: the priest had beaten the previous regional manager, on the soles of his feet, in the middle of the church... then that regional manager was removed. He must have committed a serious offence to warrant this kind of punishment; but this should not have been at the hands of the people, for such actions detract from the prestige of the state in the minds of the people.

This section to which Officer Amin Sheikho was newly appointed included a corporal who was a known troublemaker. Our officer stood at the window of the dust-covered office and watched him once again, heading up a large number of soldiers gathering in the section square where they learned of the arrival of the new regional manager; then the corporal left the men and carelessly ascended the old wooden staircase to Mohammad Amin’s office.

This corporal was the leader of subversion, and the one charged with foiling the new officer and trying to control him. Thereby the state of anarchy would continue and the level of order degenerate even further so that the French government would be compelled to transfer him away from the region and bring him back to Damascus, defeated and humiliated. By such means the French would take revenge on this free officer, Mohammad Amin, whose loyalty they doubted, though they had no evidence to prove their suspicions.

And then, the slovenly corporal entered the office of the new officer: the soldier was without his cap, his jacket was unbuttoned, and the laces of his filthy boots were left untied, as if he was mocking the officer, and had never known any sense of order.

The new officer ignored him and pretended to be reading, his head bowed, absorbed in looking at a list of names he held in his hand, ‘Corporal xxx...’ he mumbled, apparently to himself, ‘Why hasn’t he been promoted? He deserves promotion... he’s a well-disciplined active corporal and compliant to the wishes of his superiors... I shall send his name to the military authorities in order to be upgraded to sergeant.’

Here, we should point out Mohammad Amin’s clever ruse, for he was actually “thinking aloud” about the slovenly corporal who had threatened him when he first arrived and, indeed, was now standing before him.

When the corporal heard this praise and good news that he would be promoted to sergeant, he immediately set about tidying up his uniform, tying his bootlaces and buttoning up his military jacket until his appearance was much improved and he stood before the officer in a disciplined manner.

The officer had noticed what he was doing but continued with his feigned preoccupation with the list of names in his hand, and after the corporal finished tidying up his appearance, the officer raised his head saying, ‘What’s your name?’ scrutinizing him as if he did not know that he was the same person who had previously heaped abuse upon him.

‘Corporal xxx... , sir.’

In a serious, military tone of voice, the officer said, ‘Your appearance proves what I have read about your levels of discipline and obedience... yet it seems to me that you are better than the description... so, I shall put your name forward for promotion... and after a while I shall submit it again for further promotion.’

Once his words had brought the corporal under his control, our officer, Mohammad Amin, continued, ‘The police are under your command now... gather the men at once and from now on you are my right-hand man and responsible for leading them in my absence.’

The corporal acknowledged this with a perfect military salute, ‘Yes, sir.’

He left immediately to assemble the policemen and prepare the session to the best of his ability as he knew very well how to control them for he was truly worse than any of them. He then returned to tell Officer Sheikho that the men were ready for him.

The new officer went down and met with his soldiers, and gave them instructions like any officer would do when assuming his position in a new posting.

But that position was not the end with this corporal, for Mohammad Amin knew through his wide experience that the man who grows up accustomed to a life of crime and disorder cannot be reformed by gentle words, but only by discipline, humiliation, and the use of the lash. He had spent his adult life chasing criminals, imposing discipline and crushing them, and by Al’lah’s Might he had never failed.

Officer Sheikho used clever thought processes and great wisdom in all situations; and now it had become necessary to devise a plan to discipline the corporal who was currently anaesthetized to reality by the bright promises made to him.

He called three of the policemen to his side and they quickly swore their loyalty to him and he trusted them to carry out a specific task. They were distinguished by their faithfulness and whole-hearted devotion to their new officer.

One day, a full month later, the three policemen came in secret to the senior officer, Mohammad Amin, and said, ‘Sir... there is a conspiracy being plotted against you under the corporal’s leadership... they have all agreed to disobey your orders and provoke you in order to attack you and beat you up.’

Indeed, that is what the cowards agreed to do against the wise leader. But what happened in reality?

The officer answered, ‘Listen to me... I want you to arrange the morning meeting as follows: as you know, the men are lined up to form three sides of a square. I want one of you to stand on each side.’

The soldiers assembled as the commander had ordered, and when Officer Sheikho began to give his daily orders, the corporal’s voice rang out saying, ‘All of us... refuse the orders!’

Our officer pretended to be astonished, then he turned to him saying, ‘We shall see who refuse... is it all of them?... or is it only you...? Let’s start with this row.’

‘You, soldier!’ his voice boomed. And he pointed at one of the three loyal soldiers, ‘Do you refuse my orders?’

He replied in a thunderous voice, ‘No... sir!

Mohammad Amin showed no emotion as his eyes scanned the men to alight on the second loyal soldier, ‘We shall ask in the second row: you, soldier! Do you refuse my orders?’

His voice roared in denial, ‘No, sir!’

‘Now we shall ask a man in the third row: you, soldier! Do you refuse my orders?’ The third loyal soldier, like his two colleagues, replied in loud, ringing tones, ‘No... sir... only cowards refuse military orders.’

He then asked another soldier the same question; the man cowered and replied, ‘No, sir... I don’t refuse.’ And the next one replied in the same way, for at that moment they were all shrinking in fear and were afraid to utter a single word against the officer; and when he repeated the question, addressing the whole unit, they answered to a man, ‘We are all at your command, sir.’

There and then, right was established and the conspiracy was foiled; immediately the corporal began to tremble all over as he realised that his plot had failed and the soldiers had shown him no loyalty; he was alone without a single supporter, and now it was time for him to be disciplined. It was the chance for Mohammad Amin and his great plans to curb this conspirator and personally impose a fitting punishment.

‘So... you’re the only one to refuse my orders... do you dare to disobey military orders? Throw him to the ground...’ And within a minute, they had thrown him down in the dust and bound his feet to the rifle, then Officer Sheikho began to apply a severe lashing until the corporal began to cry out and appeal for help because of the terrible pain he was suffering. Then, our officer ordered the men to take the humiliated corporal to prison.

Our officer Sheikho had crushed the corporal’s tyranny and imprudent haughtiness and removed his oppressive domination of the other men, and he suppressed all of the soldiers so that they adhered to their security duties.

Mohammad Amin knew that the inhabitants of this region belonged to two sects: the Christian and the Druze. The French government favoured the Christian leaders, so he also inclined towards them rather than to the Druze sect at the beginning, until he disciplined the Druzes, with good reason, due to their wrongdoing and thereafter they submitted to the law unreservedly.

Because of his approach, the Christian brothers sent reports in praise of our officer to the French government.

Then, the Christians became complacent and began to slacken their efforts, showing clear signs of deviating from the rule of law to the extent that whereas order had stabilized amongst the Druzes it had deteriorated with the Christians; therefore he then chose to side with the Druzes against the Christians. Then, he started to implement a system of social reform until he subjected them all, both Christians and Druzes, to the authority of law and order and controlled the entire region. He beat the perverted priest on his feet, for committing a serious offence: this he did at the church, on the very spot where the priest had beaten the previous regional manager. Mohammad Amin was justified in beating him and no-one could defend him as he had been caught in the very act.

This way, the Druzes also sent reports to the French government in praise of our officer. He was, therefore, able to control both sects since the Christians could not contradict themselves by sending contrary reports.

With such great results and other similar achievements, he imposed respect for authority over the entire region, and they all submitted to the power of law and order under his command.

The people returned to their work and to their fields, and the agricultural production reached its highest level; the abundant crops filled the markets and even overwhelmed the markets of Damascus, the capital, where once there had been chaos and ruin.

Then he changed the location of the security section from the old, ramshackle building to a new one in a palace belonging to one of the tyrannical feudal lords whom he arrested while the latter was forcefully seizing the lands of oppressed farmers. He used his military powers to appropriate the property, a matter which evoked great respect for the law in the minds of all people.

To say that the French government was amazed would be to understate their reaction: how could this officer establish order and manage to control everything in such an awe-inspiring way? But the greatest surprise was to come when they sent one of their senior officers to evaluate the situation in person. After our highly successful officer, Mohammad Amin, had formally welcomed him, he found that the situation in the region was drastically changed: the security department had moved location, to cleaner, more impressive premises and was now functioning in the orderly and efficient way expected of a department of this calibre. Then the French commander asked, ‘How did this happen? I cannot believe what I see! You have achieved a miracle!’

Officer Mohammad Amin said, ‘Do you want me to order a curfew throughout the region?’

‘How can you do that? Would the people of this region, who have never submitted to the rule of law, accept a curfew being imposed on them?’ Clearly, the French officer was quite confounded by the situation which was unfolding before his eyes.

When the high-ranking French commander passed by the markets he found them bustling and noisy, and crowded with people, carriages, horses, and drovers, just as markets should be; the shops were filled with all kinds of goods, and buying and selling was constantly taking place.

Mohammad Amin had his own ideas in mind, so to prove a point he ordered a policeman to beat a drum which would announce the curfew in the markets. Just ten minutes later, after they had drunk coffee, Officer Sheikho asked the commander to take a stroll with him; they found that the previously noisy, bustling markets had come to a complete standstill; every tradesman had closed his doors and windows: silence prevailed. It was as if the entire population had been spirited away. He accompanied the French commander for a round of the main market of the county where they found the streets empty of people, and silence prevailed, as though they were walking through a cemetery. Even people from all the nearby villages had disappeared.

After the tour, and at the command of the officer, the curfew was ended by further beating of a drum, and people swarmed into the markets like locusts settling to feast on lush crops; the noise and the bustle, and the buying and selling were resumed once again, with even greater intensity than before.

The French commander was amazed; he wondered how this officer could hold sway over the policemen, the entire rebellious region and even the neighbouring districts when the French state had been defeated by them. Yes... the superior authorities had failed in their actions because of conflicting sectarian issues.

The efforts and plans of the French state had amounted to nothing, so they sent this officer to the region with a specific purpose in mind. They had doubts about his loyalty to them but had no clear evidence to support the idea, therefore they sent him to this disruptive region in the hope that he might fail in the commission; then he could be demobilized or even expelled for a legitimate reason. With that, they would be rid of him after humiliating him “but far be it from Al’lah to dishonour a righteous, merciful, honest and obedient man”. The French thought it would be most convenient if he were to be killed at the hands of the people of the region. Failing that, they wanted to get rid of him in any lawful way, but they had failed to understand the reality of this man nicknamed by the Turkish officers, and their leaders before them, Aslan which means lion.

This is the nature of the man, Mohammad Amin Sheikho, who feared none but the One and Only, the All- Supporting Al’lah.

chapters.title: The Rebellion against French Rule
chapters.html:
Mohammad Amin Sheikho agreed with the Syrian rebels that a military insurgency should be mounted against their enemy, the French, after the people of Syria suffered great cruelty, oppression and the results of corruption at their hands. They discussed this matter with him in great detail and asked him to organize the coup for them, and in case it should be discovered by the governing French, they promised to procure a plane to transport him to Iraq.

Mohammad Amin set about calling in his loyal friends from amongst the free officers, and they promised him that they would be triumphant or die in the attempt and become martyrs for their cause. He followed this by sending personal, confidential messages to the Syrian and Moroccan high-ranking officers who served in the Syrian military at that time.

To maintain their personal security he would contact them by entering a certain café which the senior officers, in particular, frequented and sit a little distance away, but in full sight of the officer to whom he had just sent a message. He would then study the officer’s facial expression to understand his reaction; if he saw the slightest signs of wonder and acceptance, he would get up from his seat and move to sit with the officer to start discussing with him the plans for the insurgency which was being planned against their oppressive enemy.

But if the officer to whom he had sent such a message appeared to be annoyed whilst reading it, and if his face showed signs of anger and incredulity, Mohammad Amin would say nothing and leave the café without any further action. In this tentative way, he was able to recruit the necessary number of approximately fifteen eminent officers, apart from his personal friends.

In the meantime, it is worth noting that it was a wellknown fact that the commander of the Moroccan division was completely subservient to the French ruling power, and that he was extremely cruel and violent towards the citizens of Syria.

One day, while Mohammad Amin was sitting in his house, he heard a knock at the door and on opening it, was surprised to find the Moroccan commander saying to him, ‘We know what you’re up to... did you think that we wouldn’t find out?’

Then our officer realised that the insurgents’ plot had been discovered and he became deeply concerned at the thought of what might happen to all those who had accepted to lead the rebellion alongside him.

The Moroccan commander entered the house with four armed men while the rest of the military unit stayed outside and surrounded the house; then he asked Mohammad Amin – the leader of the coup – to surrender and come quietly or they would have to arrest him. Our officer asked him to wait while he put on his military uniform, and added, ‘Would you take me dressed in my pyjamas?’

While changing his clothes he was searching for a solution to escape from this impasse. Many thoughts flashed through his mind in his efforts to find a way to escape this difficult situation. Then, just as he was pulling on his boots, Al’lah inspired him with a unique plan, and he said to the Moroccan commander, ‘I told the rebels just how treacherous you are and that you would take the 30,000 gold pounds that we offered you in return for your help, and that you would then turn against us... I was right! Thank God that we didn’t give you the gold in advance for we would have been deceived by you and lost it.’

As soon as Mohammad Amin uttered the phrase “30,000 golden pounds” in the hearing of the Moroccan commander, the malicious expression left his face to be replaced with a smile, and his words turned from hostility into smooth cordiality. Immediately, he ordered the four armed men accompanying him to join the force outside, and said to our honest officer, ‘Did you truly believe that I came to arrest you? No... never... you have misunderstood me. I’ve come to escort you to my office in order to work together on the plans for the coup against the infidel enemy, and as soon as we cash the gold it will be possible to launch the rebellion... so how soon can we expect to receive the gold so we can use it to set the wheels of the coup in motion? It will surely ensure its success.’

Mohammad Amin knew that the temptation of gold had made the Moroccan officer drool, for he was both greedy and treacherous and wanted the gold for himself. He planned then to approach the French and betray the leaders of the coup, so Officer Sheikho answered, ‘Would someone – a two-faced man like you – ever abandon the French and cooperate with us? I don’t think so!’

The sly Moroccan commander, afraid when faced with the truth of his actions, said, ‘On my word of honour as a military officer I’m loyal to you and would never betray you... I’ll stand by you until we are victorious. Oh Aslan! I am Muslim and the blood of Islam runs in my veins, but I was obliged to comply with the French and I was just waiting for an opportunity to rebel against them, and now is the time... so, my comrade-in-arms, you just have to bring me the gold so that the coup can get under way. Let’s shake hands on it so you can go and bring me the gold as soon as possible... let’s get rid of those French dogs.’

He stretched out his hand and our officer accepted it hesitantly saying, ‘I’m still afraid that you may betray us.’

The Moroccan commander answered him in a most unctuous manner, ‘Far be it from my mind!’

Our officer replied, ‘As long as you don’t betray us I shall bring you the gold after a week.’

The malicious, cunning commander agreed, left the house and ordered the military escort to move off with him. Thus the situation was under control... temporarily!

Having bought himself some time, our officer began to think about how to resolve the dire situation before the time came to deliver the 30,000 golden pounds: for he knew that if he failed to deliver it as promised he would certainly be arrested and executed by firing squad.

He went to the rebels and told them what had happened, asking that they send him abroad as they had promised should the coup be uncovered. However, he was very disappointed to find that the rebels were liars: they failed to procure the promised plane for him and cared nothing about him, for they only sought personal glory at the expense of his personal sacrifices and his life. Instantly he became furious and threatened them, ‘By God... by God... I will not die unless I drag all of you with me.’

Our officer left them trembling with fear and went home. He got his mother and his wife away from the house and immediately took them to a place of safety. Since the situation was now very critical and the coup might be revealed at any moment he disguised himself in woman’s clothing to avoid the imminent danger of being taken into custody and summarily executed.

He went to one of his loyal friends and gave him a full account of the situation and the threat of the death penalty hanging over his head. Without a moment’s hesitation his friend answered, ‘Welcome! This is a big house and has two floors: a ground floor and an upper one (This was the style of the houses of Damascus at that time; they consisted of two floors: the downstairs one was for summer and upstairs was used in winter). Use the upper floor and live there until the situation is resolved and you are able to leave the country; you won’t disturb me and my family because we can stay on the ground floor.’

That night, Mohammad Amin slept in his friend’s house, and in the morning the friend went to his work while his wife remained on the ground floor performing her daily tasks, and our officer remained on the upper floor. It was a very difficult situation for him as his pure, chaste spirit felt it wrong to stay alone in a house with an unrelated woman. He thought for a while then decided to leave the house, again disguised in woman’s clothing, and set off to search for another place to hide.

On Friday, he went to the mosque at which his sheikh (his mentor) Amin Kiftaru gave lessons. He sat in the private room ﴿8﴾

listening to his mentor’s sermon when he suddenly heard him saying, ‘Why are you hiding yourself? Go out, for Al’lah is to be trusted in all matters... Al’lah is the Steering One... the case is over... so why are you afraid? Go out and don’t be afraid.’

As soon as he heard these words, he took off the woman’s attire and went down openly to the group, hiding from noone, and sat listening to the sheikh’s lesson. When the lesson was over he went to bring his mother and wife and take them back to their own home.

His mother asked him, ‘What has happened that you have brought us back to the house?’

He answered, ‘My sheikh said that Al’lah is to be trusted in all matters... and the case is over.’

She said, ‘Have you risked bringing us back based simply on his words? Oh, my son... may Al’lah be pleased with you... this is not acceptable.’

He answered his mother, ‘Don’t be afraid... my sheikh said those words.’ She remained silent, against her better judgement, and they stayed in the house until Monday, the time agreed for delivering the 30,000 gold pounds.

While the honest officer was sitting in his house on Monday morning awaiting further developments, he heard a great clamour outside accompanied by the sound of the hoofs of many horses: he thought that fate had caught up with him, and if the treacherous commander did not get the money, he would certainly arrest him and have him taken off directly to be executed by firing squad. So, he climbed a tree in the courtyard to escape by way of his neighbour’s house, but as he stood on the wall between the two houses, he remembered his mother and wife, and how these criminals were used to carrying out acts of retribution by way of spoiling and robbery when the person they sought to arrest fled from the area. And a terrible thought crossed his mind that they might even violate the honour of his wife and mother; at this a storm of violent revolutionary anger and Mohammedan jealousy surged through his heart, so he leaped down from the tree, determined to fight even if he died in defence of his own honour and that of his family.

He loaded his pistol and rushed toward the door leaping over his mother who was sitting in the courtyard cleaning the grit from a dish of lentils.

He ran out to the road raising his pistol, ready to shoot to kill or be killed when his neighbour called out to him, ‘Abu Fathi! Don’t interfere... leave them alone... the leader of those Moroccan soldiers has been killed.’

There and then, he became weak at the knees on hearing this wonderful news... and he fell to the ground... overjoyed to be saved. Our officer – who was prepared to rebel for all that was right – remembered that no-one knew his secret except the Moroccan commander who sought to gain favour with the French by disclosing details of the planned coup. But in his greed, he had planned to do this only after lining his own pockets by cashing in the 30,000 gold pounds. And now, this commander had been killed and Mohammad Amin’s secret had died with him; so he thanked Al’lah and praised Him for saving him from this critical impasse.

After a while, he met with his mentor (Sheikh Amin Kiftaru) and mentioned to him the words he had heard spoken by him when he, Mohammad Amin, was in disguise in the mosque. The sheikh answered, ‘Oh, my son... I know nothing about that: it is Al’lah Who made me say those words... I do not even remember saying them... and I know nothing about the coup.’

Since that time, his mother began to give weekly alms to that veritable sheikh for him to disperse to the poor and destitute, for she respected him and looked on him with admiration and reverence as his words had proved to be true.

She knew for certain that the sheikh derived his knowledge from a pure source, so because of that terrible event she chose to adopt only the right path, with people of truth, and began to follow the ways of the saints and people of certainty. Then she reached the highest levels of truth and faith and lived a life of prosperity and fulfillment.

chapters.title: An Entire County Is Sentenced to Death
chapters.html:
The head of a military division trusts his commanding officer according to the belief and confidence he has in the man’s abilities: his cleverness and wisdom; courage and resourcefulness; sound military planning; and the successful outcomes of his timely guidance.

When the head of a division goes to war with his troops, he maintains contact with his commander, especially in the thick of battle when the scale of the war escalates and comes to a head, and when there is little or no further opportunity to change tactics or manoeuvre and he senses the actual danger surrounding the division. He can take no unilateral action so he holds the battle line and communicates with his commander via field telephone to inform him of the details of the situation and give further orders to be fulfilled at once.

Through effective communication, having considered all available information, and influenced by his own previous experience, the commanding officer guides him to a plan which he actions without delay; the outcome will then be successful, for rather than being faced with a potentially devastating defeat it can become a landslide victory. All of this is achieved by virtue of his contacting his commanding officer when the division is in a very tight corner, exactly as the Arab leader ﴿9﴾

communicated with his commander-inchief, al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf al-Thaqafi, when he had failed to conquer Bukhara, the heavily-fortified city. The commander then sent him a plan of action and he went on to conquer the city without further delay.

The examples above illustrate that if man attains true communication with God (which Al’lah wishes from all men, for their own benefit), and if he reaches this state of communication by witnessing scenes of Al’lah’s Attributes, that is, His Mercy, Sympathy, Kindness, Justice, Charity and Beauty, he would then experience real love of Him, the Almighty, since a man’s spirit is naturally disposed towards the love of perfection. Through this communication, Al’lah supplies him with the water of real life which he finds compelling, and so his prayer will keep him away from committing indecent and shameful deeds.

God says, “If only they had remained on the right path, We would certainly have supplied them with water in abundance, so that We might enthrall them by it. But if anyone turns away from thoughts of his Provider, He will cause him to undergo mounting torment.” ﴿10﴾

His heart will be filled with light through this communication by which he is able to distinguish good from evil and truth from deceit. So long as he communicates with God, turns honestly towards Him and performs the prayer by which he communicates with none but Him, this Godly Light will persist for him: it will illuminate the right path and enable him to discriminate between good and evil, for the Almighty says, “Oh you that believe! Be under Al’lah’s Light and believe in His Envoy and He will bestow on you a double portion of His Mercy and provide for you a Light by which you will walk [on the right path].” ﴿11﴾

The true believer asks for his Provider’s Guidance in all his affairs and asks to be shown the right way in every matter.

The Holy Hadith states, “The one who is obedient to Me draws ever closer to Me by performing good deeds of his own free will until I love him. If I love him, I shall be his ears by which he hears, and his eyes by which he sees.”

When man follows Al’lah’s Words (the Holy Qur’an) in every matter, he will walk in safety and tranquillity throughout this earthly life; and when he allows Al’lah’s Light to be the lamp which illuminates the way he will lead a life full of happiness and peace.

The Prophet (cpth) formed most of his battle plans whilst praying to Al’lah, as did his noble companions who came after him. Al’lah revealed the plans to him and by executing them glorious victory was achieved with the least number of casualities on both sides, for he (cpth) is the Envoy of mercy to all the worlds.

And here, we shall recount an event that took place with our merciful scholar in one of the villages of Damascus, and which proves to us the truth of the words aforementioned for “The scholars are the successors of the Prophets.”

The fires of the Great Syrian Revolution erupted in Syria and soon permeated throughout the entire territory like a powerful, uncontrollable flood, for there remained no city or village that failed to join in support of the revolution. Fighting was flaring up everywhere, and adding fuel to the fire was that the French government had been informed by its spies that a particular area of Syria had become an added burden for French forces in the country because it was a major centre of rebellion, and provided shelter for the insurgents. It supplied them with provisions and the necessary support and assistance to fulfill their revolutionary plans of destroying French interests in Syria. Added to this, most of the men of the area joined the rebels’ lines so, undeniably, they were with them, body and soul.

The reports escalated and the French government grew ever more angry and frustrated until the situation finally came to a head. When he could no longer contain his frustration and fury, the French High Commissioner decided to show his fangs and relieve his mind of the problems of this county which his spies had convinced him was a hot-bed of revolutionary movements undermining the security of France.
